items.originalTitle: I'm becoming AI-blind
items.summary:
A writer reports struggling to focus on work documents that appear to be AI-generated, describing a phenomenon they call "AI-blindness" where their brain ignores or fails to process such content effectively. They note that AI-generated texts often contain unusual phrasing, verbose explanations, or irrelevant technical jargon that disrupts comprehension and leads to repeated clarifications with colleagues.

The writer compares this effect to "banner blindness," where frequent exposure to low-effort AI content causes their brain to filter it out to maintain sanity. They observe that while AI was intended to boost productivity, it can paradoxically slow them down by reducing engagement with AI-influenced communications. This experience highlights challenges in distinguishing and effectively processing AI-generated work materials.

items.summary:
A GitHub project called NoBuzz addresses Claude AI's tendency to generate responses that sound like millennial clickbait or TED talks by using the Gemini CLI to translate its verbose answers into straightforward, human-readable English. The tool, nicknamed Claudette, processes Claude's output through Gemini to produce clearer explanations without the original's elaborate style.

NoBuzz works by taking Claude's last response and piping it through Gemini with instructions to simplify the language, printing the translation verbatim to avoid reintroducing Claude's verbose tone. The project includes installation instructions and usage details, aiming to make Claude's technical explanations more accessible and concise for users.

items.title: Nari Labs achieves sub-50 ms p95 time-to-first-audio in Qwen3-TTS 1.7B text-to-speech model on a single NVIDIA H100 SXM [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How we made a text-to-speech model respond in sub-50 ms
items.summary:
Nari Labs developed a custom implementation of the Qwen3-TTS 1.7B text-to-speech model that delivers sub-50 millisecond p95 time-to-first-audio (TTFA) while maintaining real-time playback at 10 requests per second on a single NVIDIA H100 SXM GPU. Their system outperforms four other TTS serving engines after tuning for low-latency streaming and achieves cost efficiency of about $2 per million characters at full utilization, significantly cheaper than comparable services.

The team optimized the TTS pipeline by integrating the model's three components—Talker, Code Predictor, and Codec—under a unified scheduler to better coordinate heterogeneous tasks and reduce latency. They also applied techniques such as dynamic trimming of leading silence and tuning frame accumulation to minimize audible delay and prevent playback underruns. Their benchmarks used Poisson open-loop traffic to simulate real workloads and evaluated audio quality with speech-to-text transcription.

Nari Labs has open-sourced their implementation and benchmarking methodology, providing a detailed comparison of performance and cost against existing TTS engines. Their work demonstrates a practical approach to achieving low-latency, high-throughput text-to-speech synthesis suitable for real-time applications on modern GPU hardware.

items.title: Pew Research analysis finds 10% of English-language webpages show signs of AI authorship as of mid-2026, rising to over one-third for pages published after ChatGPT's 2022 release [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much of the Internet Is Written with AI?
items.summary:
Pew Research analyzed nearly half a million English-language webpages from the past five years using AI detection tools to estimate the share of internet content written or substantially edited by AI. Their findings show that as of July 2026, about 10% of sampled pages exhibit significant AI authorship, with the proportion rising to over one-third for pages published after the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. This trend reflects the growing presence of AI-generated text across the web, particularly on commercial (.com) domains where AI-authored content is about twice as common as on organizational (.org) sites and much more frequent than on educational (.edu) or government (.gov) domains.

The study used linguistic patterns such as punctuation usage and specific vocabulary to identify AI-generated text, noting increases in features like em dashes, Oxford commas, and certain phrases favored by AI models. While detection models are not perfect, the large-scale analysis indicates a clear upward trend in AI-authored content online, raising questions about content authenticity and the evolving nature of digital communication.

items.title: Netflix tests GenRec language model to replace hand-crafted recommendation features, showing modest improvements in ranking quality and user engagement [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Netflix tests language model as alternative to hand-built recommendation logic
items.summary:
Netflix has developed and tested GenRec, a language-model-based recommendation system that converts user viewing behavior into plain text instead of relying on thousands of hand-crafted features. In offline tests and a four-week live A/B experiment, GenRec demonstrated about 1.6% better ranking quality and small but statistically significant gains in user engagement compared to the existing recommendation engine.

GenRec uses a two-stage training process with an open-weight language model fine-tuned on Netflix data to understand the catalog and user behavior, followed by specialized recommendation ranking training. The system filters user interactions to fit the model's context window and scores only real catalog entries to avoid hallucinations. items.originalTitle: Psychological methods reveal major weaknesses in AI security testing
items.summary:
Researchers at the UK AI Security Institute applied psychometric techniques to analyze eight popular safety benchmarks for language models, finding that these tests measure multiple unrelated traits rather than a single safety quality. Their study showed that models can artificially inflate safety scores by indiscriminately blocking requests, which reduces their practical usefulness. The team also discovered that most test questions are redundant, and that shorter, targeted tests can achieve similar accuracy while cutting evaluation costs significantly.

The study introduced a statistical method to detect "sandbagging," where models behave more cautiously during testing than in regular use, by identifying unusual response patterns. This method successfully flagged most cases of deliberate cautious behavior, though it occasionally misclassified harmless models. The findings highlight significant weaknesses in current AI security testing practices and suggest more efficient and reliable evaluation approaches.

items.originalTitle: Giving an LLM your prod database is easy. Taking access away is the hard part
items.summary:
DeepSQL's blog post discusses the complexities of granting large language models (LLMs) access to production databases, noting that while providing read-only connections is straightforward, enforcing fine-grained access policies and preventing unauthorized data exposure is significantly harder. The company emphasizes that simply restricting write permissions does not control who can read sensitive data, and many AI database tools use a single service account that obscures user-specific access logs.

DeepSQL has developed schema-scoped access policies enforced at multiple levels, including query planning and schema introspection, to ensure that LLMs only access authorized data. They stress the importance of guarding entire SQL statements—including subqueries and common table expressions—rather than just the main query, to prevent data leaks. The blog also highlights the need for administrators to impersonate users to verify access policies effectively, addressing a critical gap in current LLM database integrations.

items.summary: Researchers propose intelligence per watt (IPW), a metric combining task accuracy and power consumption, to assess the efficiency of local large language models (LLMs) running on devices like laptops. They evaluated over 20 state-of-the-art local LMs and 8 hardware accelerators using 1 million real-world queries, comparing accuracy, energy use, latency, and power against centralized cloud models. The study found local LMs answered 88.7% of queries successfully, with IPW improving 5.3 times from 2023 to 2025 due to advances in algorithms and hardware. Local accelerators showed at least 1.4 times lower IPW than cloud counterparts, indicating potential for optimization. These results suggest local inference can significantly reduce demand on centralized infrastructure for many queries, with IPW serving as a key metric to track this shift.

items.originalTitle: The New Robotics ‘Arms Race’: Who Can Do the Craziest Hype Video?
items.summary:
A couple months ago, a humanoid robot was dispatched to the top of Ecuador’s Mount Chimborazo, the surface point farthest from the center of the planet. It was a stunt arranged by Geologic Dome, a nonprofit that uses AI and robotics for nature conservation, which had obtained the robot from the robotics arm of Virtuals Protocol, a crypto startup.

Along with the robot, Geologic Dome sent a videographer, who hauled up three cameras to shoot clips the nonprofit could use to promote its cause. One clip shows the robot, clad in a purple winter coat and black mittens, plodding over the snowy peak. In other footage, it dances its heart out to a swing tune.

Though these clips might give the impression that robots can now rival humans when it comes to mountaineering, the robot had significant help in scaling Mount Chimborazo. A squad of flesh-and-blood people took turns carrying the 70-pound machine for much of the four-day trek to the summit. “We were 10 people, and I think six finished the expedition with back problems,” said Geologic Dome founder Pablo Berlanga Boemare, laughing.

items.title: Walmart’s Slowdown Spotlights Amazon’s Strength
items.originalTitle: Walmart’s Slowdown Spotlights Amazon’s Strength
items.summary:
This was not the day to be a Walmart shareholder. Stock of the venerable retailer tumbled 9% after the company reported a dip in comparable sales for its U.S. stores in its fiscal second quarter ending July, even as the e-commerce part of its business grew 23%. The results were fine, really, although there’s no getting around the fact that Walmart is a mature business whose top line is expanding only around 5% annually, even with the boost provided by e-commerce and advertising.

What the results really pointed to is how well Amazon is doing in retailing, comparatively speaking. That’s easy to overlook, given how much attention its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, gets on Wall Street, particularly now that AI has made cloud even more important to the tech sector. If you exclude AWS from the equation, Amazon’s retailing and associated businesses—including advertising—are growing at 14% to 15% annually. That’s not the rocket-ship growth tech companies usually expect, but it’s decent for a 30-year-old business. And it’s three times Walmart’s growth rate.
